issue.title: gateway: Node's fetch sends Sec-Fetch-Mode, so fromBrowser takes a keyed Node MCP client for a web page
issue.body:
`fromBrowser` (internal/gateway/lan.go) counts a request as a web page when it carries Origin, Sec-Fetch-Site, **Sec-Fetch-Mode** or a `Mozilla/` User-Agent. Node's built-in `fetch` (undici) sends `Sec-Fetch-Mode: cors` on every request, so a Node MCP client built on `fetch` reads as a web page.

Seen while trying Magpie Browser in Docker for real (noahhrreion's report on Discord). An MCP client on the host, using Node 22's `fetch` with a valid gateway key, POSTed to `/mcp/magpie/browser` and got 403 because the guard begins with `fromBrowser(r)`. The same call through `http.request`, which sends no sec-fetch headers, got 200 and used the browser. The same check also decides `HubVisitor.Key` and the hub's web-page refusal.

What's not known yet: whether any real agent's MCP client (the MCP TypeScript SDK's StreamableHTTP transport runs on fetch) reaches `/mcp/...` directly with these headers. Agents behind magpie's router use `magpie mcp` over stdio and aren't affected.

To decide: does a header that undici sends by itself still prove a browser? Sec-Fetch-Site, Origin and the UA are enough for real browsers. A page's script can't take Sec-Fetch-Mode off, but every browser also sends Sec-Fetch-Site with it.

comments.body:
A fix is on [the fork branch](https://github.com/skygunner/magpie/tree/fix/5522-node-fetch-browser-classification), commit [98be68098](https://github.com/skygunner/magpie/commit/98be68098a39e4ed13a8c47f48c353254e691872), based on `ed0ab567`.

`Sec-Fetch-Mode` alone no longer classifies a caller as a web page: Node fetch sends it too. `Origin`, `Sec-Fetch-Site` and Mozilla browser user agents still identify pages, and remote requests still require an enabled gateway key. The shared predicate serves Browser MCP, the hub, DNS-rebinding and remote-management guards.

A real Node **v26.13.0** process against the real `lanGuard`/gateway handler reproduced fetch=403 versus http.request=200 before the change. Afterward both return 200, and the hub runs the browser tool in the corresponding key session. Parent gateway/library authentication checks pass under `-race`, including unkeyed remote mode-only requests, valid-key browser-mark refusals, key isolation and remote proof guards. Vet, formatting and the full `nogui` build pass. The backend is a local fake; Node22 was not available, and no actual browser, full suite or cross-platform runtime was tested. AI-assisted implementation and review.

Adding a data point from a different client class, plus one refinement.

**An Electron desktop app is caught by the same guard, and cannot escape it.**

Electron/Tauri apps send `Mozilla/5.0 (Windows NT 10.0; Win64; x64) AppleWebKit/537.36
(KHTML, like Gecko) App/1.0.0 Chrome/140.0.0.0 Electron/38.0.0 Safari/537.36` by default.
Chromium lists `User-Agent` as a restricted header, so the app cannot drop the `Mozilla/`
prefix from its own network layer — an MCP client config like `"headers": {"User-Agent": "..."}`
is silently ignored (tried; the hub still saw a browser UA).

**The consequence is silent, and it is not a 403:** on `/mcp/magpie/hub` the client gets
`200 OK` with a **reduced** `tools/list` — 15 tools instead of 23. What disappears is exactly
`magpie-browser`, `magpie-image` and `magpie-memory` (8 tools). Nothing in the response says the
set was reduced, so it reads as "the Library is missing those servers".

**Measured on one Library (7 servers, 23 tools), same endpoint, only headers changed:**

| headers | tools/list | magpie-memory |
|---|---|---|
| (none) | 23 | yes |
| `Sec-Fetch-Mode: cors` | 23 | yes |
| `Sec-Fetch-Site: cross-site` | 15 | no |
| `Origin: https://example.com` | **403** | — |
| `User-Agent: Mozilla/5.0` | 15 | no |
| `User-Agent: … Chrome/140 … Electron/38 …` | 15 | no |

So on the hub path `Sec-Fetch-Mode` alone does **not** reproduce (23), while `Sec-Fetch-Site`
and any `Mozilla/` UA each do, and `Origin` refuses outright. That narrows it: the UA test is
the one signal an Electron app cannot avoid.

**Suggestion:** for the hub, drop the `Mozilla/` UA test and rely on `Sec-Fetch-Site` / `Origin`,
which a real page always sends and an Electron `net`/`fetch` client does not. If the reduced set
is deliberate (a page must not drive Browser / Image / Memory), keep it — but then say so:
a hint in the `tools/list` result, or an explicit opt-out header such as `magpie-client: full`
together with a gateway key.

Environment: magpie 0.1.4059, Windows 11, MCP router on, 7 servers in the Library.

Follow-up on the pending fix in 98be680.

That patch narrows `fromBrowser` to `Origin` / `Sec-Fetch-Site` / `Mozilla/` UA, which is right for
the Node-`fetch` case — but it does not change the Electron/Tauri case reported above: an Electron
app's UA is `Mozilla/5.0 (…) … Chrome/x Electron/y Safari/537.36`, and Chromium does not let the app
change it, so `fromBrowser` still returns true and the hub still answers with the reduced
`tools/list` (15 of 23, without `magpie-browser` / `magpie-image` / `magpie-memory`).

If keeping the UA test is deliberate — a page must not drive Browser / Image / Memory — then the
primary ask is an escape hatch: an explicit `magpie-client: full` (with a gateway key), or a hint in
the `tools/list` result saying the set was reduced. Failing that, testing `Sec-Fetch-Site` /
`Origin` only would cover it: a real page always sends both, an Electron `net`/`fetch` client sends
neither.
